local_facts.claim: New York Agriculture and Markets Law §123(10) makes the owner or lawful custodian of a dangerous dog strictly liable for medical costs resulting from an injury caused by that dog.
local_facts.why_it_matters: That medical-cost rule is narrower than many people expect. A claim for pain, lost income or other damages still commonly depends on proof that the owner knew or should have known the dog had dangerous or vicious tendencies, so the file must preserve both treatment evidence and proof of prior behavior.
local_facts.title: Medical costs and the rest of the claim are not the same question

local_facts.claim: NYC Health requires any type of animal bite to be reported within 24 hours of the event, and the city coordinates follow-up with the animal, owner and person bitten to assess rabies risk.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The Health Department report is a time-stamped public-health record that can help identify the dog and owner. It should be made promptly alongside medical care, while the separate evidence of notice, prior behavior and property control is preserved.
local_facts.title: A bite report is due within 24 hours

local_facts.claim: NYC Health reported 3,814 dog bites to city residents in 2024, the highest count in the 2015-2024 period and a 51% increase from 2015.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The citywide count underscores why a prompt Health Department report and a careful evidence record matter. A report addresses public-health follow-up; a civil claim still needs facts about the dog's prior behavior, the owner's notice and, in a building, any party with control.
local_facts.title: Reported bites reached a ten-year high in 2024

pricing.table_head: The fee schedule the First Department applies to a New York County injury claim

anchors.label: Flat ceiling under Schedule B
anchors.detail: Available only where the original retainer chose it, and choosing it gives up any later application for extra compensation.

anchors.label: Top step of the graduated Schedule A
anchors.detail: Applies to the first $1,000 recovered only, then the schedule falls to 40, 35 and finally 25 percent above $25,000.

anchors.label: Index number from the County Clerk
anchors.detail: CPLR 8018 sets $190 payable in advance plus $5 for records management and $15 for the cultural education account.

anchors.label: City license, unaltered dog over four months
anchors.detail: A spayed or neutered dog is $8.50 a year, and a lapsed license carries a $2 fine for each year it went unrenewed.

fee_rows.note: Fifty percent of the first $1,000, forty of the next $2,000, thirty-five of the next $22,000, then twenty-five percent of everything past $25,000.
The rule allows it only if the initial contract says so, and then shuts off the extraordinary circumstances application that Schedule A keeps open.

fee_rows.stage: Whether the percentage runs on net or gross
fee_rows.note: Under 603.25(e)(3) the retainer must describe both methods and show the choice, and hospital and treatment liens are never deducted first.
603.25(e)(1) treats an excess fee as the exaction of unreasonable and unconscionable compensation unless a judge authorizes it in a written order.
Judiciary Law 474-a governs medical, dental and podiatric malpractice only. A bite claim against an owner is expressly outside it.

fee_rows.stage: A claim belonging to a child
fee_rows.note: Judiciary Law 474 voids a percentage agreement with an infant's guardian unless the court, on notice, summarily values the services and orders the fee.
